doc.title: Håkan Rydin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016

title: Accompanying Pepper Adams: a dinner instead of a rehearsal
summary: Playing in the local trio behind Pepper Adams, reading his easy charts, the fast blues, and the women around him at the bar.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Did you get into accompanying those visiting jazz musicians?
Oh yes. Oh yes. I was in the local trio. I played with some nice musicians. For example I played with Pepper Adams when he was there. That was very interesting.

Well it was a musical challenge. It was nice. We met in the afternoon to rehearse what we thought. And I got his book. He was traveling by himself at that time. The book with the scores with the music. And I opened it and looked at it and it was written, you know, D flat minor in very big letters you know. Very easy to read. Four bars and four bars, and descending in red you know. So I said oh these are very good, easy, so there would be no mistakes. Then he was very, very friendly. Very laid back. And then we went to dinner. And he was an extremely slow eater. He was talking and talking and talking. It took him three or four hours. So we had a dinner and no rehearsal. So we never had a rehearsal. He
knew the scores were perfect because he used them every night. So he said there should be no mistakes.
And was there a bass player and a drummer on board also?
So you were all reading from the same book?

Yes. Well of course I knew some of it, and I knew there would be some standards, but most of it I had to read. But he didn’t pick very complicated songs. But still. I mean he started every set with an extremely fast blues. He played two choruses of melody, two choruses of solo for everyone in the group, and also he finished every set with that fast blues.

Only baritone. Yes. And then one very funny thing, in between sets we went to the bar and sat down there and maybe had a beer or something. And then in came 20 young girls, young women, just around him. I’d never seen that before. I mean he was 60 or 70 or something, bald, and looking like a bank clerk or something. But the women — it was amazing. We were just looking.
Maybe it’s the fragrance of the saxophone?
Yeah. Could be. I don’t know.
You weren’t getting the 15 or 20 women around the piano?
I was not. But I’ve got a wife of 35 years, same wife.
